A systematic craft: reconstructing the engraving sequence on a Chinese Warring States bronze yi vessel

The craft of bronze vessels from China’s Eastern Zhou period remains insufficiently understood, with prevailing assumptions that decorations were created with iron tools. This study re-examines these assumptions by applying a multi-analytical methodology, including three-dimensional digital microscopy, optical microscopy, and scanning electron microscopy with energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy, to analyze a rare engraved bronze yi vessel from the Fenshuiling cemetery, dated to the mid-Warring States period (c. 4th century BCE). The investigation identifies the vessel’s engraving tools, techniques, and sequence. Findings demonstrate the vessel consists of hot-forged, leaded tin bronze. Chasing is identified as the principal engraving technique, rather than scribing. The material’s estimated hardness supports the hypothesis that high-tin bronze tools were employed. Toolmark superposition analysis reveals a complex, multi-stage engraving process. This study provides the first science-based characterization of the engraving craft, demonstrating a systematic and scheduled approach to metal decoration that challenges previous technological interpretations.

Engraved bronze vessels are a distinctive class of artifacts from the Eastern Zhou period (771–256 BCE). Characterized by complex patterns applied to thin-walled, hot-forged bronze, they are primarily water vessels such as bronze pan plates, bronze jian basins, and bronze yi vessels1,2. The unique combination of forging and decorative techniques, together with the ceremonial nature of their motifs, has long attracted scholarly attention3,4.

The emergence of these vessels dates to no later than the mid-Spring and Autumn period. Clear evidence includes a bronze zhi vessel (M1:11) from the Xulou cemetery in Zaozhuang, Shandong province5 and two bronze dou vessels (M30:20, 21) from the Wayaopo cemetery in Xi County, Shanxi province6. During these early stages, vessel types and decorative themes varied significantly between archaeological sites. As development continued into the late Spring and Autumn period, the repertoire of vessel forms became more standardized, primarily featuring bronze yi vessels, bronze pan plates, and bronze jian basins, while their decorations exhibited greater stylistic homogeneity2. On a typical bronze yi vessel, for instance, the spout is often decorated with fish arranged head-to-tail, the main body features scenes of rituals, hunts, and chariots, and the base commonly displays intertwined serpents7.

All scientifically examined engraved bronze vessels exhibit evidence of hot-forging, with wall thicknesses typically below 5 mm5,8,9,10,11,12. This contrasts with the principle of uniform thickness that characterizes most cast bronzes from the Shang and Zhou periods13,14,15,16,17,18,19. These engraved vessels exhibit significant thickness variations across the rim, body, and base. For example, an engraved pan plate (7:281-3) from the Gaozhuang cemetery in Huaiyin of the Warring States period has a hot-forged microstructure at its base, with a thickness of 0.45–0.72 mm, whereas the rim retains its as-cast microstructure and is substantially thicker, at 1.29–2.90 mm9. This clearly indicates a manufacturing process involving casting a preform followed by hot forging.

After shaping, decorative patterns were applied using high-hardness tools, believed to be made of either bronze or iron3,20,21,22. The morphology of the tool marks is closely related to the tool tip and reveals the engraving techniques21,23. On Eastern Zhou engraved bronzes, two main types of tool marks appear: one with short, wedge-shaped lines in sequence and the other with straight lines of uniform depth3,4. These morphologies are separately associated with chasing and scribing, which may reflect chronological or regional differences20,24. It has been suggested that chasing was more common during the Spring and Autumn period (771–476 BCE), and scribing during the Warring States period (475–221 BCE).

Engraved bronze vessels from the Eastern Zhou period represent a significant technological advancement in ancient metal surface decoration. While previous studies have primarily focused on art historical perspectives, research into the specific tools and techniques for these engraved bronzes remains limited, largely due to their scarcity. Scholarship on the engraved bronze vessels from the Warring States period is particularly sparse2,11. Furthermore, the sequence in which artisans executed engraved decoration, which is crucial for understanding the craft, has also not been properly characterized25,26,27,28. This study conducts a focused, multi-analytical examination of engraving crafts from the Warring States period, aiming to identify the specific tools employed, distinguish between chasing and scribing through detailed analysis of tool marks, and reconstruct the sequence of engraving operations by examining the layering of these marks. This paper establishes a scientific framework for interpreting the engraving craft and enables a comprehensive evaluation of its historical, artistic, and technological significance.
Archaeological context and the bronze yi vessel

The Fenshuiling cemetery, located north of Changzhi in Shanxi Province, was surveyed and excavated from the 1950s to the 1970s29. The site contains over 550 tombs, of which more than 270 have been excavated, dating from the mid-Spring and Autumn period to the mid-to-late Warring States period. The quantity and diversity of artifacts offer valuable data for studying burial systems and cultural characteristics of the Eastern Zhou period30.

This study examines an engraved bronze yi vessel from Tomb M12 (mid-Warring States period) at the Fenshuiling cemetery in Changzhi, Shanxi Province. Now part of the Shanxi Museum collection (Collection No. Dong 1552), the vessel is large, thin-walled, and fragmentary (Fig. 1a). It has a wide, open spout and an inner surface decorated with finely engraved patterns of architecture, animals, trees, and human figures (Fig. 1b). The decoration survives in two main sections (Fig. 1b): an upper section near the spout with animals and plants, and a lower section with buildings and human motifs. The vessel wall is thickest at the rim, measuring approximately 3.3 mm, while the body averages a uniform thickness of 0.7 mm. The inner surface is smooth and covered by a tightly adhering greyish-green corrosion layer.
Fig. 1: The engraved bronze yi vessel from Tomb M12 at Fenshuiling cemetery.
a Overall view of the vessel. b Line drawing of the engraved decoration on the inner surface (fragmentary patterns omitted).

Due to the vessel’s fragmented condition and significance, a dual analytical strategy was used to preserve key technical and decorative information in the engraved areas. Non-destructive analysis and replication techniques were applied to the engraved surfaces, while destructive sampling was limited to non-engraved, pre-existing detached fragments.

Four small fragments were selected for destructive analysis: one from the rim and three from the body. Detailed information for each sample is provided in Table 1. These fragments were embedded in epoxy resin to prepare cross-sectional metallographic samples for optical and compositional analyses.
Table 1 Detailed information on the analyzed samples.

The morphological features of the engraved marks on the bronze yi vessel’s inner surface were observed and documented using a three-dimensional microscope (VHX-2000, KEYENCE, Osaka, Japan)31,32,33,34. Due to the vessel’s large size and uneven surface topography, direct observation was challenging in many areas. Twelve high-resolution replicas of the engraved marks were prepared from inaccessible areas using silicone rubber35,36. This replication technique enables detailed analysis of morphological features that are otherwise challenging to observe directly37,38.

For metallographic analysis, the selected bronze fragments were embedded in epoxy resin. The cross-sections were progressively ground using silicon carbide (SiC) papers (300, 600, 1500, and 3000 grit), followed by fine polishing with water-based diamond pastes39,40. The unetched microstructures were then examined using a reflected-light microscope (13XF-PC, Shangguang, Shanghai, China).

For morphological analysis of the engraved marks, the silicone rubber replicas were also embedded in epoxy resin. After hardening at low temperature, cross-sections were prepared by grinding with SiC papers (300, 600, 1500, and 3000 grit). The morphology and depth of the marks were measured using the same optical microscope.

The polished cross-sections of the bronze fragments were analyzed for their microstructure and elemental composition41,42. Analysis was performed using a scanning electron microscope (Quattro ESEM, Thermo Fisher Scientific, Waltham, MA, USA) equipped with an energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy detector (Ultim Max, Oxford Instruments, Oxford, UK). Samples were examined in high-vacuum mode at 15 kV, with an EDS acquisition time of 90–120 seconds per spectrum.

To evaluate the manufacturing techniques and assess the feasibility of various engraving tools, a comprehensive analysis of the alloy composition of the bronze yi vessel was performed. EDS analysis (Table 2) indicates that the vessel consists of leaded tin bronze, with an average composition of 11.5 wt% Sn and 6.6 wt% Pb. SEM and corresponding EDS mapping (Fig. 2) reveal that lead is distributed within the matrix as segregated lead globules (Fig. 2a, b). The EDS map for Pb demonstrates that, although lead is present as a secondary phase, it is dispersed throughout the matrix (Fig. 2b).
Fig. 2: SEM-EDS analysis of the alloy matrix.

a BSE image of the matrix in area M1. b Corresponding EDS elemental map for lead (Pb) of area M1 (indicated in cyan), demonstrating a dispersed distribution of segregated globules within the matrix. c Higher-magnification BSE image of a copper sulfide inclusion. d Higher-magnification BSE image revealing the residual (α + δ) eutectoid phase.
Table 2 EDS analysis results of the samples (wt%)

Oval-shaped inclusions are also widely distributed near the lead globules. These inclusions appear light grey under optical microscopy (OM, Fig. 3c) and display a darker contrast in back-scattered electron (BSE) imaging (Fig. 2c). EDS point analysis (Inclusion of FSL1 in Table 2) confirms that these inclusions are copper sulfide (Cu2S) particles rather than copper oxide (Cu2O). The widespread presence of these sulfides suggests the likely use of copper sulfide ores during the smelting process.
Fig. 3: Microstructure of the bronze yi vessel cross-sections.

a, b Optical micrographs of the rim (FSL1) and body (FSL3) display equiaxed grains, annealing twins, and slip lines. c Detailed OM image of oval-shaped copper sulfide inclusions. d OM image of residual (α + δ) eutectoid phase, indicating incomplete annealing.

A residual (α + δ) eutectoid phase is observed in localized regions. Under OM, the δ phase appears grey-white and surrounds yellow α-phase particles (Fig. 3d). In BSE imaging, this eutectoid structure is characterized by the lighter contrast of the δ phase encasing the slightly darker α-phase particles (Fig. 2d). EDS point analysis (Table 2) targeting the δ-phase regions confirms its distinct elemental composition. The presence of this localized residual phase indicates that the final annealing process was incomplete, likely due to insufficient temperature or inadequate holding time.

Metallographic examination provides critical insights into ancient metalworking techniques. The microstructure of the bronze yi vessel, as observed in cross-sections from both the rim (FSL1) and body (FSL3) using OM, is consistently characterized by equiaxed grains, annealing twins, and numerous slip lines (Fig. 3a, b). This thermo-mechanical grain structure demonstrates that the vessel was produced through repeated cycles of hammering (hot-forging) and annealing. Such structural evolution is fundamental in bronze metalworking for thinning vessel walls, shaping the artifact, and preventing stress-induced cracking. Additionally, the presence of dense slip lines indicates that the vessel underwent a final stage of cold working.

The discovery of iron implements at the Fenshuiling cemetery demonstrates that cast iron production was established in the Sanjin region (present-day Shanxi province) during the Warring States period29. Consequently, it has been widely assumed that the decorations on this engraved bronze yi vessel were created with iron tools. However, recent simulation experiments demonstrate that high-tin bronze tools, particularly those with approximately 20 wt% Sn, achieve superior strength and hardness for engraving22.

The morphology of the engraving marks provides direct evidence regarding the shape of the engraving tool43,44,45. Although EDS of the marks’ cross-sections could theoretically detect microscopic tool residues such as iron, direct sectioning of the engraved surface for metallographic and elemental analysis is strictly prohibited due to its destructive nature. Additionally, the vessel’s large size and uneven surface topography prevent direct examination with microscopes. To overcome these challenges, high-resolution silicone rubber replicas were produced. This non-destructive replication method accurately captures fine details in positive relief and enables safe sectioning of the replicas to reveal the cross-sectional profiles of the marks46,47.

Cross-sections of these silicone replicas consistently show a triangular profile, forming a distinct V-shape (Fig. 4). This morphology indicates that the engraving tool had a symmetrical, V-shaped tip21. Depth measurements from eight randomly selected marks on the replicas range from 14.10 μm to 32.40 μm, with an average value of 24.94 ± 6.10 μm.
Fig. 4: Cross-sectional profi le of an engraved mark on the bronze yi vessel.

Optical micrograph of a silicone rubber replica embedded in epoxy resin and sectioned perpendicular to the engraved mark. The replica (top) preserves the mark in positive relief, while the surrounding epoxy resin (bottom) supports the cross-section. The triangular, V-shaped profi le of the engraved mark indicates that the engraving tool had a symmetrical, V-shaped tip.

The presence of long, continuous straight lines initially suggested the use of scribing, a technique common during the Warring States period. However, it is essential to clearly differentiate between metalworking techniques for accurate interpretation. Scribing is a direct engraving method in which a sharp, hard tool—typically referred to as a scriber or graver— is drawn across the metal surface in any direction with equal ease and continuous pressure48. This action cuts a clean groove, reflecting a fluid, uninterrupted motion by the removal or sharp parting of the metal. Chasing, conversely, is a displacement technique rooted in plastic deformation. It employs a tracer held perpendicular to the surface, positioned on the metal, and struck intermittently with a hammer. This percussive action compresses and displaces the metal, rather than removing it, to form a groove48. Tracers with varied working ends create distinct types of marks. The effectiveness of this method relies on the hardness of the tool compared to that of the substrate, rather than the sharpness of the tracer. Therefore, if the tracer is slightly harder than the substrate, a bronze artifact can be decorated using a bronze tool.

However, detailed examination indicates that the engraving marks consist of distinct wedge-shaped and spindle-shaped impressions, which are characteristic of the chasing technique48. The shorter, wedge-shaped marks are clearly produced by chasing (Fig. 5a–c), while the longer spindle-shaped marks may be misinterpreted as scribing. These spindle-shaped marks are arranged end-to-end continuously, creating lines that appear uniform to the naked eye (Fig. 5d–f). The direction of chasing is indicated by the mark’s terminus, where the initiation point is smaller and shallower, with a width of 100–200 µm.
Fig. 5: Detailed morphology of the chasing marks is highlighted in white for clarity.

The figure compares features on the original vessel surface (negative relief) with representative examples from silicone rubber replicas (positive relief). a, b Wedge-shaped and spindle-shaped marks on the bronze surface. c A representative example of similar wedge-shaped marks on a replica. d, e Straight lines on the bronze surface, revealed to be composed of multiple long, spindle-shaped marks placed end to end. f A representative example of similar straight lines on a replica, also clearly showing its construction from constituent end-to-end marks. g, h Curved lines on the bronze surface, formed by numerous short, reoriented marks. i A representative example of similar curved lines on a replica, demonstrating the same construction method.
Analysis of the chasing marks shows that artisans employed two distinct strategies to create straight and curved elements in the design.

Straight Lines: The long, straight lines are composed of a series of elongated, spindle-shaped marks (Fig. 5d–f). The consistent orientation of adjacent marks indicates that the tool was held at a constant angle to the surface. This suggests the artisan held the chasing tool in one hand while striking its butt end with a hammer, advancing the tool forward in a straight line with each successive blow to form a continuous line.

Curved Lines: Curved lines, in contrast, are composed of short linear and punctate marks (Fig. 5g–i). The gradual change in the orientation of these individual marks creates the arc of the curve, demonstrating that the artisan was progressively adjusting the angle of the tool with each strike. Tightly radiused curves were typically formed by a multitude of short or punctate marks, while gentle arcs were formed using just two or three short linear marks.

The decorations on the engraved bronze yi vessel demonstrate a systematic and scheduled engraving sequence. The precise execution with minimal errors suggests adherence to a comprehensive design. The basis for reconstructing this sequence lies in the analysis of engraving mark superposition, which provides clear chronological indicators. The primary diagnostic criteria used in the analysis include:
The raised edges of a later mark interrupt or obscure an earlier mark (Fig. 6a), as displaced metal from the new mark fills the pre-existing one.
Fig. 6: Micrographs illustrating the three diagnostic criteria for determining superposition between chasing marks.

a Interruption: the raised edges of a later mark obscure an earlier mark. b Depth variation: a later mark is deeper than an earlier mark at their intersection. c Overshooting: the terminus of a later mark extends beyond the boundary of an earlier one.
The later mark is often deeper than the earlier one at their intersection (Fig. 6b).
The terminus of a later mark frequently overshoots the boundary set by an earlier mark (Fig. 6c).

Applying these criteria to nine representative areas on the vessel’s interior (O1–O9, Fig. 7a), a highly structured, multi-stage workflow was reconstructed. The analysis revealed a two-stage engraving sequence that progressed from spatial division to motif execution.
Fig. 7: Analysis of the operational sequence in nine representative superposition areas (O1–O9).

Earlier marks are shown in white and later marks in red. The lines indicate position only and do not represent morphology. a Location map of analyzed areas on the line drawing of the vessel interior. b–d Details showing the chronological sequence of main dividing lines. e–g Details demonstrating that individual motifs were executed after the main dividing lines. h-j Details indicating that within each motif, the outline was created before the internal details.

The process was initiated with spatial division, where the artisan engraved long, straight lines to divide the entire inner surface into decorative zones. These dividing lines were engraved in a clear, structured order (Figs. 7b–d and 8a). First, lines were drawn to separate the spout from the main body of the vessel. Next, circumferential lines were added around the rim, followed by shorter lines that further divided the larger areas into smaller decorative zones. Once spatial division was complete, the second stage, motif execution, began. Independent motifs, including plants, fish, and birds, were skillfully engraved within each decorative zone (Fig. 7e–g). The creation of each motif followed a consistent micro-sequence, progressing from the exterior contours to the internal details (Figs. 7h–j and 8b–d).
Fig. 8: Reconstructed multi-stage engraving sequence on the inner surface of the bronze yi vessel.

a Schematic of the overall workflow. The artisan first engraved long, straight lines to separate the spout from the main body and to add circumferential lines around the rim (top left), then added shorter dividing lines to subdivide the surface into smaller decorative zones (top right and bottom right), and finally executed independent motifs within each zone (bottom left). b–d Schematic representations of the consistent micro-sequence used within individual motifs, in which the exterior outline (left of each pair) was engraved before the internal details (right of each pair), illustrated for a plant, a fish, and a bird.

Based on this analysis, the complete operational sequence for the vessel’s interior decoration can be reconstructed as follows: First, divide the inner surface into decorative zones with long, straight lines; then, fill each zone with individual motifs, following an outline-to-detail sequence (Fig. 8).

Compositional analysis situates the bronze yi vessel within the metallurgical tradition of Eastern Zhou engraved vessels. Examination of 15 comparable artifacts demonstrates a deliberate, though variable, alloying strategy (Fig. 9)5,8,9,10,12,49,50. This compositional range achieves an optimal balance of tensile strength and hardness, fulfilling the requirements for ductility and formability during forging51. Bronzes with more than 9 wt% Sn meet the strength criteria for engraved bronze water containers, maintaining their shape without deformation over prolonged use, while keeping tin content below the solid solubility threshold (approximately 15.8 wt%) to prevent excessive formation of brittle eutectoid phases that would impede forging52. The presence of 6.6 wt% Pb in this bronze yi vessel enhances casting fluidity and reduces the overall hardness of the final substrate53. Microstructurally, soft lead globules dispersed throughout the matrix deform readily under localized mechanical stress from the chasing tracer54. These segregated lead inclusions significantly facilitate the plastic deformation required during engraving. In contrast, contemporaneous bronze tools typically contained 20–30 wt% Sn and less than 1 wt% Pb, resulting in substantially higher hardness than the engraved vessel substrate22. This hardness differential demonstrates the technical feasibility of employing high-tin bronze tools to engrave leaded bronze vessels.
Fig. 9: Cu–Sn–Pb ternary scatter plot comparing the alloy composition of the bronze yi vessel with previously studied Eastern Zhou engraved bronze vessels.

The composition of the bronze yi vessel from Tomb M12 at the Fenshuiling cemetery, Changzhi (this study) is plotted alongside 15 comparable engraved bronze vessels from Eastern Zhou sites across China.

Micro-morphological analysis, corroborated by the material’s confirmed ductility, necessitates a reclassification of the engraving techniques employed. Since chasing is fundamentally a displacement technique that relies on plastic deformation, the presence of soft lead inclusions within the annealed matrix facilitated this method. Long, continuous straight lines, previously identified macroscopically as scribing, a material-removal process, are now demonstrated to result from a sophisticated chasing technique. The visual effect of scribing continuity was achieved through precise control of the tool’s landing point and angle, as well as the formation of a head-to-tail connection of spindle-shaped marks. This evidence indicates an advanced level of chasing craftsmanship. This finding highlights the limitations of macroscopic classification and suggests that many bronze artifacts previously categorized as ‘line engraved’ may require microscopic re-evaluation to distinguish between material removal (scribing) and plastic deformation (chasing).

Furthermore, the reconstruction of the engraving sequence indicates that the process was highly structured and deliberately planned, rather than improvised. The workflow moved from global spatial division to local motif outlines, and then to internal details. Importantly, this systematic operational sequence was not an invention of the Warring States period, but was established as early as the mid-Spring and Autumn period. This continuity is evidenced by the engraved bronze dou vessels from the Wayaopo cemetery, where fish scales and fins clearly overlap the main body outlines11. Furthermore, the engraved bronze zhou from Yugang, Hubei, exemplifies this outline-before-detail sequence55,56. As decorative designs evolved from simple motifs on early vessels to the holistic, planned compositions seen here, this sophisticated, multi-stage workflow became increasingly essential to manage spatial layout and minimize errors.

These findings revise the traditional understanding of Warring States period engraving, revealing a sophisticated and highly systematic craft. The evidence points to a workflow involving holistic design planning, precise spatial layout, and advanced tool control. This research not only elucidates the specific craft behind a culturally and artistically significant artifact but also establishes an analytical framework for re-evaluating the technological achievements of ancient Chinese metalsmiths. Application of this integrated methodology to a broader corpus of engraved vessels promises to reveal further regional and chronological variations in this complex craft.
